title: Year three opens: the story after Acts
hookLine: the Church keeps its history honestly: holiness and failure side by side

cards: The Acts of the Apostles ends in a rented room in Rome. Paul is under guard, waiting for his case to be heard. He stays two whole years, welcoming everyone who comes, preaching without anyone stopping him.
Then the book simply stops. No verdict. No trial.
Not a word about how Paul dies, or Peter either. The Bible's story of the Church breaks off with a door open and visitors still coming in. Year three walks through that door.

teach.b: Here are the last words of Acts, in the Douay-Rheims: "Preaching the kingdom of God, and teaching the things which concern the Lord Jesus Christ, with all confidence, without prohibition."
After that, the record passes to other hands: letters, martyrs' stories, sermons, councils. That long record is church history, and this year walks through it in order.
First, the Gospels themselves don't hide the first disciples' failures. Peter, the rock, denies Jesus by a charcoal fire. The others scatter.
Paul admits he once hunted Christians down. So the story after them was never going to be clean.
Second, a parable from Matthew: the wheat and the cockle. A man sows good seed, an enemy sows weeds in the night, and the servants want to rip them out.

The master says, in the Douay, "Suffer both to grow until the harvest." Saint Augustine read that field as the Church in this age: good and bad in the same soil, sorted only at the end. Third, the year ahead.

You'll meet martyrs who forgave the crowds that killed them, monks who fed the hungry, and a woman who told a pope to go home to Rome. You'll also meet crusades, inquisitions, corrupt bishops, and the wounds of abuse.
Catholic teaching calls the Church holy because of Christ, and says plainly it is always in need of being purified, because its members sin.
A pope in our own times publicly asked forgiveness for wrongs done by Christians. Fourth, why tell it this way.
A history with only saints would be a statue, not a family.

teach.h: SUFFER BOTH TO GROW UNTIL THE HARVEST.
teach.b: Honest history lets holiness show against the real background, and leaves room for ordinary people: a bit of both.

how: Catholics learn the Church's history through the saints of the calendar, parish and family stories, and the Church's own teaching, which calls the Church holy while saying its members always need purifying and forgiveness.

games.q: you're a servant in the field. weeds have come up among the wheat overnight. what do you do?

burn the whole field and start again.
games.why: the servants want to pull them up, but the master says wait: pulling the weeds would uproot the wheat too. the sorting comes at the harvest.

practice: Go back through your family's faith as far as you can: a parent, a grandparent, a half-remembered name. Who prayed, who stopped, who kept a rosary in a drawer or walked away and came back?
Let the good and the hard sit side by side; if your family has no faith story, remember whoever first showed you kindness, and if you pray, name them before God.
